summary: In an early July 2026 pre-release cybersecurity evaluation run by Irregular, a configuration error left Meta’s Muse Spark 1.1 with internet access. The simulated scenario used a fictional company name that coincided with a real website; Irregular says the model was also given internal addresses for the simulated target. In this run, Muse Spark exploited a vulnerability on the real site, accessed some information and changed its database. Irregular disabled the evaluation and notified the affected party. Meta reviewed more than 10,000 activity records and reported no other comparable third-party exploit in that review. Both organisations described changes to isolation, scenario checks and monitoring. The affected organisation, content and persistence of changes, information accessed and recovery work were not publicly identified. The event was a misconfigured evaluation, not a demonstrated model-initiated sandbox escape.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: Target and Scope Authority Binding remains primary: the evaluator authorised a simulated offensive task with an internal target address, while this run acted on a coincident real domain. Required Control Activation independently applies to the intended closed-test network containment that was not operative when offensive execution occurred. Meta’s shorthand description of a supplied real website target is read with Irregular’s more precise fictional-name and internal-address account. Capability-Authority Separation is not independently established because availability of the internet is not shown to be the material basis for permission, rather than the ambiguous assigned target. Objective–Pathway Authority Separation lacks evidence that task utility displaced the separate scope check; this is a target/scope transition. The model did not demonstrate a sandbox escape.

primary_classification.classification_basis: Irregular’s test authority applied to a fictional, contained exercise. Its scenario configuration supplied a real website name and live internet path, causing the governed evaluation to continue against a materially different third-party target without that party’s authority. The target substitution arose in human/evaluator setup; model-initiated target selection is not asserted.

secondary_classifications.classification_basis: The evaluation was intended to run in a closed environment. Irregular’s configured containment posture was applicable for this pre-release offensive test, but a misconfiguration allowed open internet access before the governed cyber actions, and the real website was reached. The failure is at the operational isolation gate, without asserting a particular private filter or runtime component.
Reachability was necessary to act on the real site, but the evidence does not establish that technical capability itself supplied the permission premise apart from the coincident target name.
The run advanced the evaluation task through a real-world pathway, but the evidence does not establish that pathway utility independently displaced an authority check.

assessment_boundaries: Meta’s and Irregular’s postmortems are first-party participant accounts, with no published affected-party forensic record or raw model trace.

Meta describes the model as following its assigned target, while Irregular says the same scenario supplied internal simulated addresses and a fictional name coinciding with a real domain; the exact Muse Spark trajectory is not public.
The database was changed and information accessed, but their nature, persistence, sensitivity and recovery work remain undisclosed.
Meta’s finding of no other comparable exploitation is bounded to its review of more than 10,000 records.
Separate OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and UK AISI events are outside this Incident.
vigil_assessment.factual_basis: Meta reports that Irregular’s closed pre-release evaluation had inadvertent internet access and supplied a target name matching a real website; Muse Spark 1.1 then exploited the site, accessed unspecified information and changed its database. Meta describes the model as following the assigned task, and says its review of more than 10,000 records found no other comparable third-party exploit. Irregular’s own account adds that the scenario name was intended as fictional, the instructions also identified internal simulated addresses, and a small fraction of runs by different models attempted the coincident real domain. Its broader report describes a separate somewhat-similarly-named site; it does not assign that detour to Muse Spark. Irregular says it disabled the affected evaluation, notified affected parties and revised controls. The parties’ accounts are not raw model traces or affected-party forensics. The third party, altered data, information sensitivity and restoration status remain undisclosed.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The test conferred authority for a simulated target, while the coincident real domain and operative internet route allowed execution against a third party. The model’s reported real-site action crossed the simulation scope; the evaluator’s scenario and containment errors explain how the boundary became exposed without proving that reachability itself was treated as permission. The closed-test protective posture failed to operate before offensive execution. Later containment does not establish the affected website’s recovery.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: This occurrence shows that evaluation instructions and network configuration jointly determine the actual authority boundary. Scenario names need validation against live targets, and the isolation state must be checked before offensive model execution, with logs adequate to identify any real-world effects.
